title: Bengaluru Startup Unveils Static Prototype of AI-Piloted Fighter With Planned 1,500 Km Range
excerpt: Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace showed the full-scale FWD Supreme in New Delhi. Its 350-kg payload, Mach 0.85 speed and 1,500-km range are design targets for an aircraft that has not yet flown.
body:
• Bengaluru startup Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace has unveiled a full-scale static prototype of the FWD Supreme, billed as India's first indigenous AI-piloted autonomous fighter aircraft.
  • All performance figures are planned, not demonstrated: a 350-kg payload, Mach 0.8-0.85 top speed, 500-600 kmph cruise and a range above 1,500 km for the 1.5-tonne Heavy variant, which has not flown.
  • The smaller 250-kg Supreme Lite has completed taxi trials and is being prepared for a first flight, with certification steps planned in the next two months.
  • The company says the full programme needs about $100 million; $7 million has been raised toward the $10 million light version.

Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA), a Bengaluru-based startup, has unveiled a full-scale static prototype of the FWD Supreme, an AI-piloted autonomous fighter aircraft it is developing in India. The company presented the aircraft at Le Méridien in New Delhi, outlining a family of uncrewed combat aircraft built around Indian design, engineering and manufacturing, according to The Machine Maker. The company itself is at fwdefence.com.

Senior defence officials attended the unveiling, including A. Anbarasu, Additional Secretary and Director General (Acquisition) in the Ministry of Defence, Air Marshal Prem Kumar, Lieutenant General Puneet Ahuja and Major General Tarun Aggarwal. Anbarasu congratulated the company on what he called a "wonder bird" but advised it to move forward in a calibrated and coordinated manner, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.

Planned Specifications — Not Yet Flown

The FWD Supreme Heavy is a 1.5-tonne-class aircraft in a flying-wing configuration, roughly 10 metres by 10 metres, with an internal weapons bay and a coating intended to give it stealth qualities. Its proposed specifications, released by the company, are a payload capacity of 350 kg, 5 kN of thrust from twin engines, a maximum speed of Mach 0.8 to 0.85, a cruising speed of about 500-600 kmph, a range of 1,500 km and endurance of more than two hours, with satellite communications planned.

https://x.com/SwarajyaMag/status/2110300830851309998

Those numbers describe a design target, not a tested aircraft. Chief Technology Officer Girish G. Dixit, a former member of the Aeronautical Development Agency team that developed the LCA Tejas, told BusinessLine the Heavy's configuration has been frozen and its detailed design is about halfway complete. The aircraft is also designed to navigate in GPS-contested environments using visual odometry — estimating position from sequences of camera images — and the company has tied up with the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, for quantum applications and data encryption.

"With Manik engine, we will have 80 per cent Indian content and without that, it will come down to 60 per cent."

— Suhas Tejaskanda, Founder & CEO, Flying Wedge

The Smaller Test Bed Comes First

The programme's near-term workhorse is the 250-kg Supreme Lite. Dixit said key technologies for the Heavy will be sourced from the lighter aircraft, which will act as a test bed as well as a standalone product. The Lite has completed taxi trials and is being prepared for its first flight, which the company expects within the next two months, after which it will pursue certification from the Centre for Military Airworthiness & Certification (CEMILAC) and NATO, according to BusinessLine. The Lite is described as about 90% indigenous and uses an engine manufactured by UMS in Coimbatore.

For the Heavy, founder and CEO Suhas Tejaskanda said the company will try to use DRDO's in-house Manik engine and, if that does not work, look abroad, with Czech company PBS among the probable options. Barring the engine and some sensors, he said, the content will be indigenous.

Funding and the Mobbing Idea

Tejaskanda was direct about why a static prototype was shown at this stage: as a startup, pooling funds is a huge challenge, and investors want to see phased development and quality validation. He put the cost of developing the FWD Supreme at $100 million, of which $10 million would go to the light version, for which $7 million has been raised. The fundraising also involves the company's Kaal Bhairava programme, an AI-powered medium-altitude long-endurance autonomous combat aircraft that he said has completed 100 hours of trial flying.

FWDA also outlined a "Mobbing Doctrine," in which multiple AI-enabled aircraft operate in coordination and share information, rather than relying solely on a small number of high-value crewed platforms. Through its Operation 777 initiative, the company plans to work with international partners while building domestic capability.

What to Watch

The test for the programme is sequential and public: a first flight for the Lite, certification steps, and then progress on the Heavy's detailed design and engine choice. Until the Lite flies, the FWD Supreme remains what it was presented as — a static prototype with an ambitious specification sheet, from a startup attempting to enter a field BusinessLine noted only the US, China and Turkey are currently contesting.
